Get started with energyRt

Source: vignettes/energyRt.Rmd
energyRt.Rmd

Describe the energy system with reusable components

A comprehensive, modular energy system modeling framework with an R interface.

An energy system is a network of flows. Resources are extracted or harvested, converted by technologies, moved, stored, and consumed as useful energy. Planning that system means deciding what to build, when to build it, and how to operate it while meeting demand and respecting physical and policy constraints.

energyRt is a framework and macro-language for stating that problem in R. Modelers describe commodities, technologies, supply, demand, storage, and trade as reusable objects. energyRt uses those objects to generate the sets, mappings, equations, and solver inputs required by its implementations, then reads the solution back into R.

The package provides modeling machinery rather than a fixed model, dataset, or scenario. The same components can support a small teaching example, a national planning model, or a detailed multi-sector study.

How it works: bricks, time, and space

An energyRt model combines reusable bricks with explicit time and space structures:

  • Bricks describe commodities and processes. They are inspectable R objects that can be drawn, updated, reused, and combined in repositories.
  • Time comes from a modeler-defined nested timescales calendar. Annual, seasonal, hourly, representative, and sampled resolutions are choices, not package limits. A full 8,760-hour year is one possible calendar; it is not a fixed requirement or ceiling.
  • Space comes from a nested geoscales hierarchy. National, zonal, and nodal balances can coexist, with each commodity and process placed where its data belongs. Time, space, and the planning horizon belong to the model configuration rather than to every process definition. A technology can therefore be reused with a different calendar or geographical hierarchy when its data support that change. Solver backends are discussed separately below: they are maintained implementations of the energyRt formulation, not another structural axis.

The central object types are:

Brick Constructor Role
commodity newCommodity() an energy carrier or accounting flow
technology newTechnology() converts inputs into outputs
supply newSupply() provides a resource at an availability and cost
demand newDemand() defines consumption that must be met
storage newStorage() moves a commodity between timeslices
trade newTrade() moves a commodity between regions or the rest of the world
weather newWeather() supplies exogenous profiles such as capacity factors
repository newRepository() collects reusable bricks
model newModel() binds a repository to time, space, and a horizon
scenario interpolate() / solve() materializes and solves one model configuration

A technology connects input -> use -> activity -> output; costs, capacity, availability, emissions, and auxiliary flows attach to that chain. The model bricks article develops the complete object system.

A five-minute model

The first model has one fuel, one power plant, and one electricity demand. The units and timeframe are explicit: annual energy is measured in PJ, capacity in GW, and costs in MEUR.

GAS <- newCommodity(
  name = "GAS",
  desc = "Natural gas",
  timeframe = "ANNUAL",
  unit = "PJ"
)
ELC <- newCommodity(
  name = "ELC",
  desc = "Electricity",
  timeframe = "ANNUAL",
  unit = "PJ"
)

gas_supply <- data.frame(
  cost = 6.0
)
SUP_GAS <- newSupply(
  name = "SUP_GAS",
  desc = "Natural gas supply",
  commodity = "GAS",
  unit = "PJ",
  supply = gas_supply
)

gas_efficiency <- data.frame(
  comm = "GAS",
  cinp2use = 0.55
)
gas_investment <- data.frame(
  invcost = 900
)
EGAS <- newTechnology(
  name = "EGAS",
  desc = "Combined-cycle gas power plant",
  input = list(comm = "GAS"),
  output = list(comm = "ELC"),
  ceff = gas_efficiency,
  invcost = gas_investment,
  fixom = 25,
  cap2act = 31.536,
  olife = 25L
)

electricity_demand <- data.frame(
  demand = 50
)
DEM_ELC <- newDemand(
  name = "DEM_ELC",
  desc = "Annual electricity demand",
  commodity = "ELC",
  unit = "PJ",
  demand = electricity_demand
)

draw(object = EGAS)

Collect the bricks, define a planning horizon, bind the model to one region, and solve it with the bundled GLPK solver:

HELLO_REPOSITORY <- newRepository(
  name = "HELLO_REPOSITORY",
  GAS,
  ELC,
  SUP_GAS,
  EGAS,
  DEM_ELC,
  desc = "Components of the introductory electricity model"
)

HELLO_HORIZON <- newHorizon(
  name = "HELLO_HORIZON",
  desc = "Planning horizon from 2025 through 2040",
  period = 2025:2040,
  intervals = c(1, 5, 10),
  mid_is_end = TRUE
)

HELLO <- newModel(
  name = "HELLO",
  desc = "Single-region gas-to-electricity model",
  data = HELLO_REPOSITORY,
  region = "R1",
  discount = 0.05,
  horizon = HELLO_HORIZON
)

BASE <- solve_model(
  object = HELLO,
  name = "BASE",
  solver = solver_options$glpk,
  echo = FALSE
)

solve_model() interpolates and solves in one call. The composable form exposes the intermediate scenario when it needs to be inspected or modified:

BASE_STAGED <- HELLO |>
  interpolate(name = "BASE_STAGED") |>
  solve()

Results return as tables at the same level of detail as the model:

base_objective <- getData(
  object = BASE,
  name = "vObjective",
  merge = TRUE
)
base_capacity <- getData(
  object = BASE,
  name = "vTechCap",
  merge = TRUE
)

base_objective
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   scenario name       value
#>   <chr>    <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 BASE     vObjective 6677.
base_capacity
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   scenario name     tech  region  year value
#>   <chr>    <chr>    <chr> <chr>  <int> <dbl>
#> 1 BASE     vTechCap EGAS  R1      2025  1.59
#> 2 BASE     vTechCap EGAS  R1      2030  1.59
#> 3 BASE     vTechCap EGAS  R1      2040  1.59

The model built 1.59 GW of gas capacity—enough to supply 50 PJ per year under the declared conversion efficiency. The solved scenario also contains every underlying flow, cost, and balance.

Plot solved results

autoplot() uses the same result tables returned by getData(). On a solved scenario it can show annual generation, capacity, new capacity, fuel use, or storage operation. The annual electricity balance from BASE is:

generation_plot <- autoplot(
  object = BASE,
  type = "generation",
  comm = "ELC"
)
generation_plot

The capacity view reads the same scenario without another solve:

capacity_plot <- autoplot(
  object = BASE,
  type = "capacity"
)
capacity_plot

Sub-annual models add a dispatch view by selecting timeslices, for example autoplot(object = scenario, type = "generation", timeslice = "^SUM_").

Save, find, and reload scenarios

An energyRt project stores scenarios, their runs, and references to their model inputs. save_scenario() writes the scenario and adds it to the project registry. The name can then be used instead of a path:

BASE <- save_scenario(
  object = BASE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
#> Scenario 'BASE' saved in 'C:/Users/admin/AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpkpDSSr/energyRt-intro/BASE-HELLO-HELLO_HORIZON'
#> Directory size: 0.24 MB

project_registry <- load_registry()
project_registry[, c("type", "name", "parent")]
#> # A tibble: 15 × 3
#>    type     name  parent
#>    <chr>    <chr> <chr> 
#>  1 model    HELLO ""    
#>  2 scenario BASE  ""    
#>  3 run      glpk  "BASE"
#>  4 scenario BASE  ""    
#>  5 run      glpk  "BASE"
#>  6 scenario BASE  ""    
#>  7 run      glpk  "BASE"
#>  8 scenario BASE  ""    
#>  9 run      glpk  "BASE"
#> 10 scenario BASE  ""    
#> 11 run      glpk  "BASE"
#> 12 scenario BASE  ""    
#> 13 run      glpk  "BASE"
#> 14 scenario BASE  ""    
#> 15 run      glpk  "BASE"

BASE <- load_scenario(
  path = "BASE",
  env = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE
)

registered_objective <- getData(
  object = "BASE",
  name = "vObjective",
  merge = TRUE
)
registered_objective
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   scenario name       value
#>   <chr>    <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 BASE     vObjective 6677.

load_scenarios() loads several registered scenarios as a named list, while scenario_runs() lists the solves recorded inside one scenario. Arrow-backed storage allows result tables to remain on disk until they are queried. See Scenario management for the registry, object stores, variants, and portable project bundles.

Sample a calendar

Sampling changes the temporal representation of a scenario. It is useful for rapid exploration, but it is an approximation unless the chosen slices are representative. A sample must retain complete members of a calendar level; calendar_samples() builds valid sample specifications and records how much of the year each one covers.

data(
  list = "topia",
  package = "energyRt"
)
s4_h24 <- topia$modules$calendars$s4_h24

SEASON_SAMPLES <- calendar_samples(
  calendar = s4_h24,
  level = "SEASON",
  sample_size = 2,
  n = 2,
  method = "random",
  seed = 2050
)
SEASON_SAMPLES
#> calendar_samples: 2 sample(s), method = random
#>   slices per sample: 48-48 | distinct slices used: 96

solve_by_sample() interpolates and solves each sample, preserving the sample definition and its runs. This larger TOPIA example is not executed while the introductory vignette builds:

TOPIA_KIT <- topia$modules$electricity$R1
TOPIA_SAMPLING <- newModel(
  name = "TOPIA_SAMPLING",
  desc = "TOPIA model used to demonstrate calendar sampling",
  data = TOPIA_KIT$repo,
  calendar = s4_h24,
  region = TOPIA_KIT$regions,
  horizon = topia$modules$horizons$base,
  discount = 0.05
)
TOPIA_SAMPLING <- setGeoscale(
  obj = TOPIA_SAMPLING,
  geoscale = TOPIA_KIT$geoscale
)

TOPIA_SAMPLES <- solve_by_sample(
  object = TOPIA_SAMPLING,
  name = "TOPIA_SAMPLES",
  samples = SEASON_SAMPLES,
  solver = solver_options$glpk,
  echo = FALSE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
sample_summary(
  x = TOPIA_SAMPLES,
  name = "vTechCap",
  by = "tech"
)

See Time resolution and Workflow for manual calendar subsets, weighting, repeated samples, and comparisons with a full solve.

One formulation, several maintained backends

energyRt contains implementations of its formulation in several modeling languages. A model object can be compiled through any implementation available in the local environment, but this is concrete package support rather than backend independence in the abstract: each route works because energyRt ships and maintains code for it.

Route What the energyRt implementation does Good fit
GLPK / MathProg writes MathProg and solves with bundled glpsol first models, teaching, reproducible local runs
Julia / JuMP writes JuMP for HiGHS, CBC, GLPK, CPLEX, or cuOpt larger local models and Julia solver environments
Python / Pyomo writes Pyomo for HiGHS, CBC, GLPK, or CPLEX Python-based solver environments
GAMS writes the formulation in GAMS established institutional GAMS workflows
multimod (experimental) constructs an in-memory model in multimod’s R DSL/AST, then assembles an LP/MPS matrix, solves with HiGHS, or renders equations as LaTeX; it is not a separate text modeling language matrix workflows, inspection, and mathematical documentation
mmcloud (experimental) submits large matrix problems to cloud infrastructure and solves them with GPU-capable backends models that exceed local memory or compute capacity

Check the toolchains before selecting an optional route. en_check_dependencies() is read-only; solve = TRUE additionally verifies configured backends by solving a small test model.

backend_status <- en_check_dependencies(
  solver_pkgs = TRUE,
  solve = FALSE
)

julia_components <- c("Julia", "Julia packages")
julia_rows <- backend_status$component %in% julia_components
julia_found <- backend_status$found[julia_rows]
julia_ready <- length(julia_found) == length(julia_components)
julia_ready <- julia_ready && all(julia_found)

if (julia_ready) {
  BASE_JULIA <- solve_model(
    object = HELLO,
    name = "BASE_JULIA",
    solver = solver_options$julia_highs,
    echo = FALSE
  )
}

pyomo_rows <- backend_status$component == "Pyomo"
pyomo_ready <- isTRUE(backend_status$found[pyomo_rows])

if (pyomo_ready) {
  BASE_PYOMO <- solve_model(
    object = HELLO,
    name = "BASE_PYOMO",
    solver = solver_options$pyomo_cbc,
    echo = FALSE
  )
}

NEOS provides another remote route for supported solvers without a local license. The solver backends article covers installation, presets, dependency checks, and operational limits.

Generate reports

report() renders object datasheets and model or scenario reports. A scenario report includes solve status, generation and capacity charts, costs, and other available results; a process report documents its declared parameters and diagram. HTML reports require Pandoc, so these calls are shown but not executed during the vignette build:

base_report <- report(
  object = BASE,
  format = "html",
  open = FALSE
)

gas_plant_report <- report(
  object = HELLO,
  name = "EGAS",
  format = "html",
  open = FALSE
)

Reports are cached against the object, template, and arguments; unchanged inputs do not trigger another render. The Reports article covers full scenario reports, process groups, levelized costs, and HTML/PDF/Word output.

From one solve to a study

The first solve uses only a fraction of the framework:

  • Build and reuse. update() derives variants without duplicating complete formulations; repositories organize components into model libraries.
  • Represent detail where it matters. Nested timeframes and geographies let different commodities and processes balance at different levels.
  • Scale the formulation. Sparse interpolation materializes only the tuples used by a scenario; vintages, clusters, graded resources, and custom constraints extend the model without changing its workflow.
  • Manage many runs. Named projects and Arrow-backed scenario folders keep results addressable and allow larger-than-memory analysis.
  • Inspect and validate. draw(), autoplot(), report(), and verify_solution() expose both declared objects and solved behavior.
  • Analyze in R. Results flow directly into dplyr, ggplot2, and the rest of the R ecosystem without a separate export-import step.

TOPIA, the teaching model shipped with energyRt, connects these ideas in a multi-region electricity system with nested geography and time, storage, trade, capacity expansion, dispatch, and policy scenarios.
